content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes DropAut and its variants (UnitsDropAut and BottleneckDropAut). They learn the dropout probabilities from one or two linear layers instead of using a preset hyperparameter, and can replace dropout layers easily. Experiments on different datasets and network architectures demonstrate their effectiveness over the original dropout, despite all on relatively small scales.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

-- The methods can make the network regularization strength adaptive to the datasets its dealing with, so that human tuning for the drop probability may be avoided. Given the drop probability is an important hyperparameter to tune, the methods have practical use cases.

-- The experiments are quite extensive, with datasets ranging from vision to NLP tasks and architectures from MLP, CNN to Transformers. 

Weaknesses:

-- The method still has hyperparameters to set - min and max drop probabilities. Sometimes they have a large effect. In Table 3, not setting them can lead to large performance decrease, but setting them may defeat the purpose of eliminating dropout hyperparameters.

-- The experiments are too small in scale. MNIST and CIFAR improvements in such scales and upon such low baseline levels (e.g., 86% on CIFAR-10) may not be significant enough to demonstrate the methods' effectiveness in a general and modern setting. 

-- It seems the vanilla dropout's drop rates are not tuned in the experiments. The vision transformer drop rate of 0.1 is inherited directly without further tuning on CIFAR-100. The default drop rate was not designed for CIFAR-100 but for much larger datasets. This puts a huge disadvantage to the vanilla dropout baselines. The paper also noted this "This means that the model benefits from using drop rates even lower than 0.1, or potentially not using Dropout at all" but did not take actions to address it.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper was well written and easy to understand. The method seems novel and different from prior works as far as I know. The code link is not accessible for now.
content.summary_of_the_review: The methods are interesting and well-motivated but I don't think the experiment section has demonstrated their true superiority compared with the vanilla dropout. Therefore I recommend "marginally below".
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a family of dropout layers that can learn the drop/keep probability during training. Because the probabilities are learned and set automatically, the resulting architectures are named DopAut for automatic dropout. Three variants of DropAut are presented and evaluated on rather small datasets, but on fully connected and convolutional networks as well as transformers.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

Learning the drop probability during training is interesting and potentially impactful, since setting it up hand is ineffective or requires extensive trial and error. 

Applicability to CNNs and transformers is clearly a strength of the proposed methodology.

The study on the benefits of accounting for the dropped activations at training or test time may be useful to other researchers working on similar topics.

Experiments are described in detail and the analysis is useful. Figure 2 for example is a nice illustration of overfitting.

Weaknesses

Some design choices are not explained well. For example, it is unclear why the AD networks were implemented with a single linear layer, except for Bottleneck DropAut, which has two linear layers. 

The experiments are not fully convincing. The datasets are rather small for modern standards, while the number of classes in MNIST, CIFAR-10 and IMDb Movie Reviews dataset is definitely small. The differences in accuracy are in most cases very small. Different labels are assigned to a single-digit number of the 10,000 training examples. (Table 2 is a good example of this. The comment that follows it that “UnitsDropAut and BottleneckDropAut show good improvements over both the Baseline and the classic Dropout” is exaggerated.) It is hard to argue that all other factors are held equal, and these differences are only due to differences in dropout strategies. Differences in network capacity may be equally important, for example.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is very well written and the methods can be reproduced based on the description. Code will be made available when the paper is accepted.

The review of related work is brief, but the cited papers are explained well in the context of the proposed approach. There are, however, several omissions from the related work section. The following come to mind.
[A] Zhengsu Chen, Jianwei Niu, Xuefeng Liu, and Shaojie Tang. Selectscale: Mining more patterns from images via selective and soft dropout. In International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence, pages 523–529, 2020.
[B] Golnaz Ghiasi, Tsung-Yi Lin, and Quoc V Le. Dropblock: A regularization method for convolutional networks. In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, pages 10727–10737, 2018.
[C] Gao Huang, Yu Sun, Zhuang Liu, Daniel Sedra, and Kilian Q Weinberger. Deep networks with stochastic depth. In European Conference on Computer Vision, pages 646–661, 2016.
[D] Saihui Hou and Zilei Wang. Weighted channel dropout for regularization of deep convolutional neural network. In AAAI, pages 8425–8432, 2019.
[E] Ambar Pal, Connor Lane, René Vidal, and Benjamin D. Haeffele. On the regularization properties of structured dropout. In IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, pages 7668–7676, 2020.
[F] Hieu Pham and Quoc V. Le. Autodropout: Learning dropout patterns to regularize deep networks. In AAAI, pages 9351–9359, 2021.
[G] Baifeng Shi, Dinghuai Zhang, Qi Dai, Zhanxing Zhu, Yadong Mu, and Jingdong Wang. Informative dropout for robust representation learning: A shape-bias perspective. In International Conference on Machine Learning, pages 8828–8839, 2020.
[H] Andrea Zunino, Sarah Adel Bargal, Pietro Morerio, Jianming Zhang, Stan Sclaroff, and Vittorio Murino. Excitation dropout: Encouraging plasticity in deep neural networks. International Journal of Computer Vision, 129(4):1139–1152, 2021.

Disabling units of the network and setting activations to zero may be interpreted as not perfectly equivalent. I have seen interpretations where disabling units of the network means that backpropagation through them is also disabled, which is not the case for zeroed out activations. I do not doubt the correctness of the method, but the text should be a little more precise.


Minor Comments

Section 2, par. 2 and elsewhere: “fully-connected networks” is more precise than “feedforward” to distinguish from CNNs and transformers.

Section 3, last sentence: the final random variables are not independent since they are generated by increasing the dimensionality after the bottleneck. 

I do not see much value in the term “stuff training.”
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is interesting as it proposes a novel dropout methodology, which is applicable to CNNs and transformers. My comments on lack of clarity in the design of the AD networks and the omissions in the literature review section can be addressed in the rebuttal and by a relatively minor revision. What I find less satisfactory is that the benefits of the proposed dropout layers are small compared to standard dropout. The largest difference is on the binary IMDb Movie Reviews dataset, which seems to have been selected for this purpose. It is possible that the accuracy on MNIST is saturated, and differences are hard to observe. I would like to see a response from the authors on this in the rebuttal.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a DROPAUT to prevent the model overfitting. The DROPAUT apply a layer to learn the dropping operation. Several experiments on MNIST, CIFAR, and IMDB MOVIER EVIEWS datasets shows the effectiveness of this method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
The paper has a clear organization and writing. 
This paper propose a data-driven method to learn the dropping operation.
Several experiments are conducted to show the effectiveness of the method.

Weakness:
There is a lack of theoretical analysis: since the drop out operation is to prevent data-driven model learning from overfitting; then whether there is a contradiction in motivation to learn drop out? 
The experiment dataset is too small, there should be more experiments on larger-scale dataset. Further, the performance improvement is tiny From Table.3. It needs the mean and variance of multiple experimental results. 
It needs more related method comparison.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper has a very clear organization and expression. And the paper proposes a data-driven method to learn the dropping out operation, that the idea is very simple.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper proposes a DROPAUT to prevent the model overfitting. And several experiments on MNIST, CIFAR, and IMDB MOVIER EVIEWS datasets shows the effectiveness of this method.
However, the idea is simple and seems to have a contradiction with the overfitting.
Moreover, experiments on larger-scale dataset and multi-experiment results should be provided.
To sum up, this paper is a well-written paper but lack of the valuable research points.
